lesson.title: When the Two Sides Disagree: Jump Discontinuity
lesson.summary: A jump discontinuity happens when both one-sided limits exist but land on different values, so the function genuinely leaps from one level to another instead of approaching a single number.
lesson.body:
A discontinuity at c is called a jump discontinuity when both one-sided limits, lim(x to c-) f(x) and lim(x to c+) f(x), exist as finite numbers but are not equal to each other. Because the two sides disagree, the ordinary two-sided limit lim(x to c) f(x) does not exist at all, no matter what value f(c) happens to take. Unlike a removable discontinuity, there is no single patch value that could fix a jump discontinuity, since fixing the left side would break the right side and vice versa. The function has genuinely different behavior approaching from each direction.

The size of the jump, the difference between the right-hand limit and the left-hand limit, is a meaningful number in its own right, and it is often what makes jump discontinuities useful rather than just a nuisance. Step-like real-world quantities, a parking garage rate that increases at the top of every hour, a shipping cost that increases at weight thresholds, or a tax bracket that changes at an income cutoff, are naturally modeled with jump discontinuities, since the quantity genuinely leaps rather than sliding smoothly from one value to the next.

Worked example: let f(x) = floor(x), the greatest integer function, and examine x = 3. For x in [2, 3), f(x) = 2, so lim(x to 3-) f(x) = 2. For x in [3, 4), f(x) = 3, so lim(x to 3+) f(x) = 3. Both one-sided limits exist and are finite, 2 and 3, but they are not equal, so lim(x to 3) f(x) does not exist, and f has a jump discontinuity at x = 3 with jump size 3 - 2 = 1. Since f(3) = 3 matches the right-hand limit, f is right-continuous at 3, using the one-sided continuity language from earlier, even though it is not continuous there in the full two-sided sense.

A second example: define f(x) = -1 for x < 0 and f(x) = 1 for x >= 0. Approaching from the left, lim(x to 0-) f(x) = -1. Approaching from the right, lim(x to 0+) f(x) = 1. Both limits exist and are finite, but -1 does not equal 1, so this is a jump discontinuity at x = 0 with jump size 1 - (-1) = 2. Because f(0) = 1 matches the right-hand limit, f is right-continuous at 0 but not left-continuous, and therefore not continuous, matching the same pattern as the floor function above.

Jump discontinuities connect directly to one-sided limits, since checking for one requires computing lim(x to c-) f(x) and lim(x to c+) f(x) separately and then comparing them, rather than trying to evaluate a single two-sided limit that will not exist. This is also the discontinuity type most clearly distinguished from what comes next, infinite discontinuity, where instead of two different finite values, at least one side runs off toward positive or negative infinity rather than settling anywhere at all.

A jump discontinuity can be right-continuous, left-continuous, or neither, depending entirely on which one-sided limit, if any, happens to match f(c). In the floor function example, f(c) always matches the right-hand limit, so floor is right-continuous everywhere despite its jumps. A different piecewise definition could just as easily match the left-hand limit instead, or match neither, leaving f discontinuous from both directions at once even though both one-sided limits still exist as finite numbers.
